paras: The threatened lynching of the Wilkin brothers took place at Breeze, Illinois, in late October 1888, when Henry, Ben and John Wilkin, arrested for stabbing a man in a saloon row, were reported to have narrowly escaped being lynched. No one was killed, and the episode survives only in a one-sentence item in the Indianapolis Journal.

According to the Indianapolis Journal, the three Wilkins were charged with "assaulting and stabbing John Swartz in a saloon row on Sunday." The item ran among Illinois news datelined October 23, which places the Sunday of the fight on or about October 21. The paper said the brothers were "under arrest at Breeze" and added that they "narrowly escaped being lynched."

The report gave no account of who threatened the brothers, how many people took part, or whether the threat came before or after their arrest. Nor did it state the race of the Wilkins or of Swartz, or say how badly Swartz was hurt.
No report of a trial, of Swartz's recovery or death, or of any action against those who threatened the brothers appears in the coverage.

The Indianapolis Journal printed the item on October 24, 1888, in the "Brief Mention" column of its "Indiana and Illinois News" page, between notices of a county lawsuit over bridge materials and a school closing for a throat illness. It carried no headline of its own and no comment, treating the near-lynching as one more minor regional note. No other paper in the collection was found to carry the story.
